0.title: Zephaniah: He Will Rejoice Over You
0.overview:
Zephaniah begins with God sweeping the earth bare and ends with God singing. No book in the Bible travels further in three short chapters.

The prophet traces his family four generations back to Hezekiah (1:1), probably the king, which would make him a member of the royal house and a relative of the king he preached to. He preached in the days of Josiah, the boy king who later tore down the idols of Judah (2 Kgs 22:1-2; 23:5). Since the idolatry Zephaniah attacks is still in full swing, he probably spoke before those reforms, and may well have helped to spark them.

Chapter 1 announces the great day of the LORD. It is a day of wrath, distress, darkness and trumpet blast, and it falls first on God's own people. Zephaniah walks his hearers through their own city as it falls, gate by gate and district by district. He names three kinds of people God will deal with: those who openly worship other gods, those who bow down and swear to the LORD and yet swear by Milcom (1:5), and those who simply drifted and do not seek the LORD or inquire of him (1:6). The most memorable picture in the chapter is God going through Jerusalem with lamps, searching out people who are not wicked so much as settled, who say in their hearts, The LORD will not do good, nor will he do ill (1:12).

Chapter 2 opens a door. Before the day comes, there is one thing to do: Seek the LORD, all you humble of the land ... seek righteousness; seek humility; perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the LORD (2:3). Then judgment sweeps round the compass, from the Philistine coast to Moab and Ammon, to Cush and finally to Nineveh, the city that said, I am, and there is no one else (2:15).

Chapter 3 turns back to Jerusalem, where the officials are lions, the judges wolves, the prophets treacherous and the priests careless with holy things, while The LORD within her is righteous and shows his justice each dawn (3:5). Then God says, wait for me (3:8), and everything changes. He purifies the speech of the peoples so that they call on his name together, leaves a people humble and lowly who take refuge in him, and tells Zion to sing.

The book's summit is 3:17: The LORD your God is in your midst, a mighty one who will save; he will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing. Many Christians can believe that God tolerates or forgives them. This says that God is glad about them, that his love quiets them as a parent quiets a frightened child, and that he sings over them. It is one of the most startling verses in the Old Testament, and it is spoken to the same city God had promised to search with lamps.

Two themes tie the book together. The first is the day of the LORD, near and certain, when silver and gold will deliver nobody (1:18). The second is the humble remnant: not the officials or the rich, but ordinary people who seek God, take refuge in his name, and are hidden on that day.

Zephaniah points to Christ at both ends. The judgment he describes is real, and Peter reminds Christians that they were ransomed not with perishable things such as silver or gold (1 Pet 1:18) but with Christ's blood. And the promise that The King of Israel, the LORD, is in your midst (3:15) came true when a child was named Immanuel, which means God with us (Matt 1:23). The purified speech of the nations began at Pentecost and ends with a crowd from every tribe and language before the throne (Rev 7:9). And the God who sings over his people is the God whose Son endured the cross for the joy that was set before him (Heb 12:2) — the joy, in the end, of having them.

So this small book asks a simple question of every reader. Which of the three groups in chapter 1 do you belong to: the openly idolatrous, the hedgers, or the drifters? And it gives the same answer to all three: seek the LORD while he may be found, and discover that the God you feared is the God who is glad to have you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The word comes to Zephaniah in the days of Josiah (v. 1): I will utterly sweep away everything from the face of the earth, man and beast, birds and fish (vv. 2-3). God's hand stretches out against Judah and Jerusalem, against the remnant of Baal, the rooftop star-worshippers, those who swear both by the LORD and by Milcom, and those who simply stopped seeking him (vv. 4-6).
verseByVerse.theology: God's judgment begins with his own people, and includes those who add other gods to him as well as those who quietly drift away.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD that came to Zephaniah the son of Cushi, son of Gedaliah, son of Amariah, son of Hezekiah, in the days of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah. "I will utterly sweep away everything from the face of the earth," declares the LORD. "I will sweep away man and beast; I will sweep away the birds of the heavens and the fish of the sea, and the rubble with the wicked. I will cut off mankind from the face of the earth," declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the LORD that came to Zephaniah the son of Cushi, son of Gedaliah, son of Amariah, son of Hezekiah, in the days of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah.

Zephaniah gives a longer family tree than any other prophet, four generations back to Hezekiah. That is probably King Hezekiah, which would make Zephaniah a member of the royal family and a distant cousin of the king he preached to. He had access, and he used it to say hard things.

He preached in the days of Josiah, the good king who came to the throne as a boy and later purged the country of idols (2 Kgs 22:1-2; 23:5). The idolatry Zephaniah describes was still in full operation, so he probably preached before those reforms, and his message may well have helped to bring them about.

"I will utterly sweep away everything from the face of the earth," declares the LORD.

"I will sweep away man and beast; I will sweep away the birds of the heavens and the fish of the sea, and the rubble with the wicked. I will cut off mankind from the face of the earth," declares the LORD.

The book opens at full volume. Listen to the order of the creatures: man and beast, the birds of the heavens, the fish of the sea. That is the creation account of Genesis 1 read backwards (Gen 1:26). Sin does not merely break rules; it unmakes the world, and God's judgment lets it run to its end.

The rubble with the wicked is a striking phrase (the ESV notes it may mean "stumbling blocks", that is, idols). The idols people served go into the skip alongside the people who served them.

Before we hurry past this, notice that the book which ends with God singing over his people begins here. The Bible's comfort is never cheap. It is spoken to people who have first been told the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: "I will stretch out my hand against Judah and against all the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and I will cut off from this place the remnant of Baal and the name of the idolatrous priests along with the priests, those who bow down on the roofs to the host of the heavens, those who bow down and swear to the LORD and yet swear by Milcom, those who have turned back from following the LORD, who do not seek the LORD or inquire of him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I will stretch out my hand against Judah and against all the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and I will cut off from this place the remnant of Baal and the name of the idolatrous priests along with the priests,

God's hand stretches out first against his own people. The remnant of Baal suggests that Baal worship had already been cut back, perhaps by earlier reforms, and God intends to finish the job. Half-cleared idolatry is still idolatry.

Notice also the idolatrous priests along with the priests: the pagan clergy and the official clergy are both named. When God judges a nation he starts with its religion.

those who bow down on the roofs to the host of the heavens, those who bow down and swear to the LORD and yet swear by Milcom,

Now three kinds of people are described, and most of us are somewhere in the list.

First, the frank pagans: those who go up on the flat roofs at night to worship the host of the heavens, the sun, moon and stars. Josiah later removed exactly these priests (2 Kgs 23:5).

Second, and more subtly, those who bow down and swear to the LORD and yet swear by Milcom, the god of Ammon (the ESV notes this may be read "their king"). These are the hedgers. They have not left the faith; they have added to it. They attend the temple and keep another god in reserve, in case God fails them. It is a deeply modern position.

those who have turned back from following the LORD, who do not seek the LORD or inquire of him."

Third, the drifters. No other god is mentioned here at all. They simply stopped: they do not seek the LORD or inquire of him. No dramatic apostasy, no decision to walk away. Prayer thinned out, then stopped. God names this alongside star-worship, which should trouble anyone whose faith has quietly gone cold.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — A Sacrifice and a Search
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Be silent before the Lord GOD! He has prepared a sacrifice and consecrated his guests (v. 7). Officials, the king's sons and the violent traders will be punished (vv. 8-11). I will search Jerusalem with lamps, says God, hunting out the complacent who say The LORD will not do good, nor will he do ill (v. 12). They will build houses and never live in them (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: Nothing escapes God's search, least of all the comfortable unbelief that assumes he does nothing at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Be silent before the Lord GOD! For the day of the LORD is near; the LORD has prepared a sacrifice and consecrated his guests. And on the day of the LORD's sacrifice— "I will punish the officials and the king's sons and all who array themselves in foreign attire. On that day I will punish everyone who leaps over the threshold, and those who fill their master's house with violence and fraud. "On that day," declares the LORD, "a cry will be heard from the Fish Gate, a wail from the Second Quarter, a loud crash from the hills. Wail, O inhabitants of the Mortar! For all the traders are no more; all who weigh out silver are cut off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be silent before the Lord GOD! For the day of the LORD is near; the LORD has prepared a sacrifice and consecrated his guests.

Be silent before the Lord GOD! Habakkuk, preaching around the same time, ended his second chapter with the same hush (Hab 2:20). There is a point at which argument stops and the court falls quiet.

Then a chilling image. God has prepared a sacrifice and consecrated his guests. In Israel a sacrifice was usually followed by a feast. But who is on the table? Judah itself. The guests invited to the meal are the invading armies. Revelation uses the same terrible picture of the last battle, where birds are called to the great supper of God (Rev 19:17).

And on the day of the LORD's sacrifice— "I will punish the officials and the king's sons and all who array themselves in foreign attire.

On that day I will punish everyone who leaps over the threshold, and those who fill their master's house with violence and fraud.

God names names. The officials and the king's sons: the governing class, Zephaniah's own relatives. Foreign attire is not about fashion; dressing like the surrounding nations was a public statement about whose culture and whose gods you admired.

Leaping over the threshold was probably a pagan superstition; we read of the priests of Dagon avoiding a threshold in Philistia (1 Sam 5:5). And then the plain charge: servants who fill their master's house with violence and fraud (the ESV notes this may read "their Lord's"). Superstition and dishonesty travel together, because both are attempts to control life without God.

"On that day," declares the LORD, "a cry will be heard from the Fish Gate, a wail from the Second Quarter, a loud crash from the hills.

Wail, O inhabitants of the Mortar! For all the traders are no more; all who weigh out silver are cut off.

Zephaniah takes his hearers on a tour of their own city as it falls: the Fish Gate in the north wall where the invaders would enter, the Second Quarter where the well-to-do lived, and the Mortar, probably the hollow of the market district. The sound moves from a cry to a wail to a loud crash.

And the business district falls silent: all the traders are no more; all who weigh out silver are cut off (the ESV notes the phrase may mean "all the people of Canaan", a term for merchants). Judgment reaches the shops and the banks, not only the temples.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time I will search Jerusalem with lamps, and I will punish the men who are complacent, those who say in their hearts, 'The LORD will not do good, nor will he do ill.' Their goods shall be plundered, and their houses laid waste. Though they build houses, they shall not inhabit them; though they plant vineyards, they shall not drink wine from them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At that time I will search Jerusalem with lamps, and I will punish the men who are complacent, those who say in their hearts, 'The LORD will not do good, nor will he do ill.'

Here is one of the great images of the Bible. God comes through the city with lamps, like a man searching a cellar, bending into every corner. Nobody is overlooked because they are unimportant.

And what is he looking for? Not the murderers first, but the men who are complacent. The ESV notes that the Hebrew pictures wine left undisturbed until it thickens on its dregs: settled, unstirred, going thick.

Then their creed, and it is not atheism: The LORD will not do good, nor will he do ill. They believe God exists. They simply do not believe he does anything. He is retired, or distant, or uninterested, and therefore life can be arranged without reference to him.

That is probably the most common form of unbelief inside churches. Not a denial of God, but a settled assumption that he will not actually intervene, judge or act. Zephaniah says God takes a lamp and goes looking for exactly those people.

Their goods shall be plundered, and their houses laid waste. Though they build houses, they shall not inhabit them; though they plant vineyards, they shall not drink wine from them."

The sentence is the old covenant curse, which Amos and Micah had also announced (Amos 5:11; Mic 6:15). The comfortable life they were quietly trusting in will not be enjoyed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The great day of the LORD is near, near and hastening fast (v. 14): A day of wrath ... a day of distress and anguish ... a day of darkness and gloom (vv. 15-16). People will walk like the blind because they sinned against the LORD (v. 17), and Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: The day of the LORD is certain, near and beyond the reach of money.

verseByVerse.quote: The great day of the LORD is near, near and hastening fast; the sound of the day of the LORD is bitter; the mighty man cries aloud there. A day of wrath is that day, a day of distress and anguish, a day of ruin and devastation, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and thick darkness, a day of trumpet blast and battle cry against the fortified cities and against the lofty battlements. I will bring distress on mankind, so that they shall walk like the blind, because they have sinned against the LORD; their blood shall be poured out like dust, and their flesh like dung. Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them on the day of the wrath of the LORD. In the fire of his jealousy, all the earth shall be consumed; for a full and sudden end he will make of all the inhabitants of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The great day of the LORD is near, near and hastening fast; the sound of the day of the LORD is bitter; the mighty man cries aloud there.

Now the drumbeat begins. Near, near and hastening fast. This is not a distant theological possibility; it is coming at speed.

And notice who is crying: the mighty man, the professional soldier, the one who is supposed to be steady when everyone else panics.

A day of wrath is that day, a day of distress and anguish, a day of ruin and devastation, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and thick darkness,

a day of trumpet blast and battle cry against the fortified cities and against the lofty battlements.

Six times in two verses: a day. The repetition is the point; the hammer falls again and again. From the Latin of verse 15 comes the name of the medieval hymn Dies Irae, "day of wrath", which the church sang for centuries.

A Christian should read these verses in two directions. They describe the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, which happened exactly as described. And they describe the last day, of which that fall was a small rehearsal.

I will bring distress on mankind, so that they shall walk like the blind, because they have sinned against the LORD; their blood shall be poured out like dust, and their flesh like dung.

People will grope about like the blind, with no idea where to go. And the reason is stated without decoration: because they have sinned against the LORD. Their blood and flesh, so precious to them, will be treated as dust and dung.

Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them on the day of the wrath of the LORD. In the fire of his jealousy, all the earth shall be consumed; for a full and sudden end he will make of all the inhabitants of the earth.

The last verse removes the final hope of the men in the Second Quarter: Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them. Money can buy an escape from most things; it buys nothing here. Proverbs says the same: Riches do not profit in the day of wrath (Prov 11:4).

Peter tells Christians what did deliver them: you were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your forefathers, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Pet 1:18). The day of wrath is real, and there is exactly one shelter from it. The next chapter will name it.

1.title: The Great Day of the LORD
1.overview:
The word of the LORD comes to Zephaniah, whose family is traced back to Hezekiah, in the days of Josiah (v. 1). God announces that he will utterly sweep away everything from the face of the earth: man and beast, birds and fish, the rubble with the wicked (vv. 2-3). He will stretch out his hand against Judah and Jerusalem, cutting off the remnant of Baal, the idolatrous priests, those who worship the host of heaven on the roofs, those who swear both to the LORD and by Milcom, and those who have simply turned back from following him (vv. 4-6).

Let all be silent, for the day of the LORD is near and he has prepared a sacrifice and consecrated his guests (v. 7). He will punish officials, the king's sons, those in foreign attire, those who leap over the threshold and fill their master's house with violence and fraud (vv. 8-9). Cries will be heard from the Fish Gate, the Second Quarter and the Mortar, and the traders will be cut off (vv. 10-11). God will search Jerusalem with lamps to punish the complacent who say the LORD will do neither good nor ill; their houses and vineyards will be taken from them (vv. 12-13).

The great day of the LORD is near and hastening fast, a day of wrath, distress, ruin, darkness, clouds and trumpet blast against the fortified cities (vv. 14-16). People will walk like the blind because they have sinned against the LORD, and neither silver nor gold will deliver them in the fire of God's jealousy (vv. 17-18).
1.theology:
Sin unmakes creation, and God's judgment lets that unmaking run its course (vv. 2-3; Gen 1:26).

Judgment begins with God's own people and with their religion (vv. 4-5; 1 Pet 4:17).

Dividing our trust between God and a second god is as serious as open paganism, and quiet drift is named alongside both (vv. 5-6).

There is a point where argument ends and silence before God is the only response (v. 7; Hab 2:20).

God searches out the comfortable unbelief that assumes he will never act (v. 12).

The day of the LORD is near, certain and terrible, and the fall of Jerusalem was its rehearsal (vv. 14-16).

Wealth cannot buy deliverance on that day; only the ransom God provides can (v. 18; Prov 11:4; 1 Pet 1:18).
1.examples:
The creation account of Genesis read backwards.

Idols thrown out with the people who served them.

Worshippers who swear by God on the Sabbath and keep a second god in reserve.

People who never walked out, whose praying just thinned out and stopped.

A sacrifice where the guests are invading armies.

God going through a city with a lamp, looking into corners.

Wine left so long undisturbed that it thickens on its dregs.

Silver and gold that buy nothing at all on one particular day.

What a desolation she has become, a lair for wild beasts! Everyone who passes by her hisses and shakes his fist.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Perhaps You May Be Hidden
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gather together, says the prophet to a shameless nation, before the day of God's anger comes (vv. 1-2). Then the one command that can still save: Seek the LORD, all you humble of the land ... seek righteousness; seek humility; perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the LORD (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The only shelter from the day of wrath is God himself, and the door stands open to the humble.

verseByVerse.quote: Gather together, yes, gather, O shameless nation, before the decree takes effect —before the day passes away like chaff— before there comes upon you the burning anger of the LORD, before there comes upon you the day of the anger of the LORD. Seek the LORD, all you humble of the land, who do his just commands; seek righteousness; seek humility; perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gather together, yes, gather, O shameless nation,

before the decree takes effect —before the day passes away like chaff— before there comes upon you the burning anger of the LORD, before there comes upon you the day of the anger of the LORD.

After the thunder of chapter 1 comes an urgent appeal. Gather together: call a solemn assembly, get the people to God. And the word before beats four times. There is still time, and it is running out. (The ESV notes the Hebrew of takes effect is "gives birth": the decree is like a pregnancy, quietly advancing to a fixed day.)

They are called a shameless nation, which is the problem exactly. A nation that could still be ashamed could still be saved quickly.

Seek the LORD, all you humble of the land, who do his just commands; seek righteousness; seek humility; perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the LORD.

Here is the heart of the chapter, and the only advice that matters when God's judgment is coming. Three times: seek.

Seek the LORD: not an experience, not safety, but God himself. Seek righteousness: the just dealing that chapter 1 found missing in the market. Seek humility, which is an odd thing to chase and impossible to boast about having found.

The call goes to all you humble of the land (the ESV notes their description may read "who carry out his judgment"): not the officials or the wealthy of chapter 1, but the ordinary poor who still did what God said. God has never been short of such people, and they are usually invisible.

And then that careful word: perhaps you may be hidden. Not "you will certainly escape". Zephaniah will not turn God's mercy into a mechanism. Other prophets speak the same way: Who knows whether he will not turn and relent (Joel 2:14), it may be that the LORD ... will be gracious (Amos 5:15), and the king of Nineveh's Who knows? (Jonah 3:9). This is not doubt about God's kindness; it is the refusal to presume on it.

The word hidden is beautiful, though. The psalmist knew it: he will hide me in his shelter in the day of trouble (Ps 27:5). There is a hiding place on the day of wrath, and it is a person. For us that person has a name, and those who are in Christ are hidden in him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod and Ekron will be emptied, and the seacoast will become pasture for the remnant of the house of Judah (vv. 4-7). God has heard the taunts of Moab and the revilings of the Ammonites, and they will become like Sodom and Gomorrah for their pride (vv. 8-10). He will famish all the gods of the earth, and the nations will bow to him, each in its place (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: God judges the mockers of his people and then gathers the nations he has humbled.

verseByVerse.quote: For Gaza shall be deserted, and Ashkelon shall become a desolation; Ashdod's people shall be driven out at noon, and Ekron shall be uprooted. Woe to you inhabitants of the seacoast, you nation of the Cherethites! The word of the LORD is against you, O Canaan, land of the Philistines; and I will destroy you until no inhabitant is left. And you, O seacoast, shall be pastures, with meadows for shepherds and folds for flocks. The seacoast shall become the possession of the remnant of the house of Judah, on which they shall graze, and in the houses of Ashkelon they shall lie down at evening. For the LORD their God will be mindful of them and restore their fortunes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Gaza shall be deserted, and Ashkelon shall become a desolation; Ashdod's people shall be driven out at noon, and Ekron shall be uprooted.

Now Zephaniah turns to the nations, moving round the compass: west, east, south, north. He starts west with the Philistine cities, Israel's oldest neighbours and enemies. Driven out at noon suggests an attack so confident that it comes in broad daylight, when armies usually rest.

Woe to you inhabitants of the seacoast, you nation of the Cherethites! The word of the LORD is against you, O Canaan, land of the Philistines; and I will destroy you until no inhabitant is left.

And you, O seacoast, shall be pastures, with meadows for shepherds and folds for flocks.

The busy coastal plain, full of fortified cities and trade, will become quiet grazing land (the ESV notes meadows may be "caves"). Sheep will crop grass where the markets were.

The seacoast shall become the possession of the remnant of the house of Judah, on which they shall graze, and in the houses of Ashkelon they shall lie down at evening. For the LORD their God will be mindful of them and restore their fortunes.

And there, quietly, is the first promise of the book: the remnant of the house of Judah. God will have a people left, and they will lie down safely in the very houses of their old enemies. The LORD their God will be mindful of them: he has not forgotten, even when the news is all judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have heard the taunts of Moab and the revilings of the Ammonites, how they have taunted my people and made boasts against their territory. Therefore, as I live," declares the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, "Moab shall become like Sodom, and the Ammonites like Gomorrah, a land possessed by nettles and salt pits, and a waste forever. The remnant of my people shall plunder them, and the survivors of my nation shall possess them." This shall be their lot in return for their pride, because they taunted and boasted against the people of the LORD of hosts. The LORD will be awesome against them; for he will famish all the gods of the earth, and to him shall bow down, each in its place, all the lands of the nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I have heard the taunts of Moab and the revilings of the Ammonites, how they have taunted my people and made boasts against their territory.

East of the Jordan lay Moab and Ammon, descendants of Lot, related to Israel and endlessly hostile. Their sin here is not invasion but mockery: taunts, revilings, boasts. And God says, I have heard.

There is comfort in that for anyone who has been sneered at for their faith or their failures. Words spoken against God's people are not lost in the air; they are heard in heaven.

Therefore, as I live," declares the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, "Moab shall become like Sodom, and the Ammonites like Gomorrah, a land possessed by nettles and salt pits, and a waste forever. The remnant of my people shall plunder them, and the survivors of my nation shall possess them."

Moab and Ammon lay near the Dead Sea, in the country where Sodom and Gomorrah had been overthrown (Gen 19). Their own neighbourhood was the warning they ignored. Now nettles and salt pits, the vegetation of ruined ground, will take their fields.

This shall be their lot in return for their pride, because they taunted and boasted against the people of the LORD of hosts.

The verdict names the root: their pride. Mockery is pride with a voice.

The LORD will be awesome against them; for he will famish all the gods of the earth, and to him shall bow down, each in its place, all the lands of the nations.

A remarkable verse. God will famish the gods, starving them of the sacrifices that kept their temples running, until they simply fade away. And then the horizon opens: to him shall bow down, each in its place, all the lands of the nations.

Notice each in its place. They will not all have to travel to Jerusalem. Worship will reach the nations where they live, which is exactly what Jesus told the woman at the well: the hour was coming when true worshippers would worship the Father neither on her mountain nor in Jerusalem, but in spirit and truth (John 4:23).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Cush will fall by God's sword (v. 12), and Assyria too: he will make Nineveh a desolation, a dry waste like the desert, with owl and hedgehog lodging in her ruined columns (vv. 13-14). This is the exultant city that lived securely, that said in her heart, "I am, and there is no one else." Now passers-by hiss and shake the fist (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: A city that claims God's own "I am" for itself ends as a ruin where wild birds nest.

verseByVerse.quote: You also, O Cushites, shall be slain by my sword. And he will stretch out his hand against the north and destroy Assyria, and he will make Nineveh a desolation, a dry waste like the desert. Herds shall lie down in her midst, all kinds of beasts; even the owl and the hedgehog shall lodge in her capitals; a voice shall hoot in the window; devastation will be on the threshold; for her cedar work will be laid bare. This is the exultant city that lived securely, that said in her heart, "I am, and there is no one else." What a desolation she has become, a lair for wild beasts! Everyone who passes by her hisses and shakes his fist.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You also, O Cushites, shall be slain by my sword.

South now, to Cush, the region beyond Egypt. One short line for a distant people, which is the point: distance is no protection.

And he will stretch out his hand against the north and destroy Assyria, and he will make Nineveh a desolation, a dry waste like the desert.

And north to the superpower itself. Nineveh, the capital of the world, will become a dry waste like the desert. Nahum preached the same message at length; here it takes three verses. Nineveh fell in 612 BC, within a few decades of these words.

Herds shall lie down in her midst, all kinds of beasts; even the owl and the hedgehog shall lodge in her capitals; a voice shall hoot in the window; devastation will be on the threshold; for her cedar work will be laid bare.

The picture is unforgettable: wild animals sleeping in the streets, birds nesting on the carved capitals at the tops of the palace columns, something hooting from an empty window frame (the ESV notes that the identity of the animals rendered owl and hedgehog is uncertain, and that all kinds of beasts is "beasts of every nation"). The costly cedar work, imported from Lebanon at ruinous expense, lies open to the weather.

This is the exultant city that lived securely, that said in her heart, "I am, and there is no one else." What a desolation she has become, a lair for wild beasts! Everyone who passes by her hisses and shakes his fist.

Here is the epitaph, and the boast in it is the blasphemy of the ancient world. I am, and there is no one else is almost word for word what God says about himself through Isaiah: I am the LORD, and there is no other (Isa 45:5). Babylon would later say the same and fall for it (Isa 47:8).

That is what self-sufficiency finally claims, whether a superpower says it or a heart says it quietly: there is no one else who matters, and I answer to nobody. The chapter ends with tourists hissing at the ruin.

And this is why verse 3 stands where it does. Between the judgment of Judah and the judgment of the nations, God put an open door: Seek the LORD, all you humble of the land. The proud city said I am; the humble say He is, and are hidden.

2.title: Seek the LORD, All You Humble
2.overview:
The shameless nation is called to gather before the decree takes effect and the burning anger of the LORD arrives (vv. 1-2). The humble of the land, who do God's commands, are told to seek the LORD, seek righteousness and seek humility; perhaps they will be hidden on the day of his anger (v. 3).

Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod and Ekron will be deserted; the seacoast of the Philistines will become pasture, and the remnant of Judah will possess it, for the LORD will be mindful of them and restore their fortunes (vv. 4-7). God has heard the taunts of Moab and the revilings of Ammon, and swears they will become like Sodom and Gomorrah, a waste of nettles and salt pits, plundered by his remnant, because of their pride (vv. 8-10). He will famish all the gods of the earth, and every land will bow to him, each in its place (v. 11).

The Cushites will fall by his sword (v. 12), and he will stretch out his hand against the north to make Nineveh a desolation, where herds lie down, owl and hedgehog lodge in her capitals and a voice hoots in the window (vv. 13-14). This is the exultant city that said in her heart, "I am, and there is no one else", and now everyone who passes by hisses and shakes a fist (v. 15).
2.theology:
There is a "before" in God's dealings: warnings are given while there is still time to turn (vv. 1-2).

Seeking God himself, with righteousness and humility, is the only shelter on the day of wrath (v. 3; Ps 27:5).

God's mercy may be sought but never presumed upon: "perhaps you may be hidden" (v. 3; Joel 2:14; Amos 5:15; Jonah 3:9).

God hears what is said against his people, and mockery is pride with a voice (vv. 8, 10).

God starves the idols of the nations and gathers worshippers from every land, each where they are (v. 11; John 4:23).

Distance and power are no protection from God (vv. 12-13).

Self-sufficiency finally claims God's own name for itself, and ends in ruin (v. 15; Isa 45:5; 47:8).
2.examples:
Four urgent "befores" in a single sentence.

An invisible community of humble people God has never been without.

A promise that says "perhaps", and means it.

Sheep grazing where the Philistine markets used to be.

Taunts spoken about God's people and heard in heaven.

Gods starved of sacrifices until they fade away.

An owl nesting on the carved top of a palace column.

A city whose last word was "I am".

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Woe to her who is rebellious and defiled, the oppressing city! She listens to no voice and accepts no correction (vv. 1-2). Her officials are roaring lions, her judges evening wolves, her prophets treacherous and her priests profane (vv. 3-4) — while The LORD within her is righteous, showing his justice each dawn (v. 5). God cut off other nations as a warning, and still they were eager to make all their deeds corrupt (vv. 6-7). Therefore wait for me (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: God's steady daily justice stands in the middle of a corrupt city, and the call to his people is to wait for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to her who is rebellious and defiled, the oppressing city! She listens to no voice; she accepts no correction. She does not trust in the LORD; she does not draw near to her God. Her officials within her are roaring lions; her judges are evening wolves that leave nothing till the morning. Her prophets are fickle, treacherous men; her priests profane what is holy; they do violence to the law. The LORD within her is righteous; he does no injustice; every morning he shows forth his justice; each dawn he does not fail; but the unjust knows no shame.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to her who is rebellious and defiled, the oppressing city!

She listens to no voice; she accepts no correction. She does not trust in the LORD; she does not draw near to her God.

After Nineveh, we expect another foreign capital. But the oppressing city is Jerusalem. God's own city gets the same woe as Assyria's.

Verse 2 lists four failures, and they read like a diagnosis of spiritual decline in any life. She listens to no voice: God has spoken and she will not hear. She accepts no correction: rebuke bounces off. She does not trust in the LORD: she relies on politics and money instead. She does not draw near to her God: prayer has stopped. Deafness, defensiveness, distrust, distance.

Her officials within her are roaring lions; her judges are evening wolves that leave nothing till the morning.

Her prophets are fickle, treacherous men; her priests profane what is holy; they do violence to the law.

Four groups of leaders, and every one has failed. Officials who should protect are roaring lions. Judges are evening wolves, ravenous at dusk and leaving nothing by morning. Prophets are unreliable and treacherous, saying whatever suits. Priests handle holy things carelessly and do violence to the law, twisting God's word to get their way. Micah had said the same of the same city a century before (Mic 3:9-11).

The LORD within her is righteous; he does no injustice; every morning he shows forth his justice; each dawn he does not fail; but the unjust knows no shame.

And then this quiet, beautiful verse in the middle of the corruption. The LORD within her is righteous. He has not left the city. While the judges devour and the priests twist, God is still in the middle of it all, doing right.

Every morning he shows forth his justice; each dawn he does not fail. Like the sunrise, without exception, day after day. Jeremiah's Lamentations says it of his mercies: they are new every morning (Lam 3:23).

The last line is the tragedy: but the unjust knows no shame. God's daily faithfulness changes nothing in them. It is possible to live in a city where God is visibly good and to feel nothing at all.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have cut off nations; their battlements are in ruins; I have laid waste their streets so that no one walks in them; their cities have been made desolate, without a man, without an inhabitant. I said, 'Surely you will fear me; you will accept correction. Then your dwelling would not be cut off according to all that I have appointed against you.' But all the more they were eager to make all their deeds corrupt. "Therefore wait for me," declares the LORD, "for the day when I rise up to seize the prey. For my decision is to gather nations, to assemble kingdoms, to pour out upon them my indignation, all my burning anger; for in the fire of my jealousy all the earth shall be consumed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I have cut off nations; their battlements are in ruins; I have laid waste their streets so that no one walks in them; their cities have been made desolate, without a man, without an inhabitant.

God points to the ruins on the horizon. Other nations have already fallen, and those ruins were meant to be read: empty streets, broken walls, cities left without a man, without an inhabitant.

I said, 'Surely you will fear me; you will accept correction. Then your dwelling would not be cut off according to all that I have appointed against you.' But all the more they were eager to make all their deeds corrupt.

Here is the sorrow of God, expressed as a thwarted hope: Surely you will fear me. (The ESV notes the Hebrew reads "her" where the ESV has your.) He judged other nations partly so that his own people would learn without having to suffer the same.

And they drew the opposite conclusion: all the more they were eager. Warnings that do not soften us harden us. That is a sober thing to hold next to the news, where other people's disasters are on display every day.

"Therefore wait for me," declares the LORD, "for the day when I rise up to seize the prey. For my decision is to gather nations, to assemble kingdoms, to pour out upon them my indignation, all my burning anger; for in the fire of my jealousy all the earth shall be consumed.

This is the hinge of the chapter, and the command is startling: wait for me. Chapter 1 said the day of wrath was coming; now God tells the faithful to wait for that very day. For those who belong to him, the day of judgment is not a threat to dread but a rescue to expect.

Everything up to here has been the problem. Everything after it is what God will do. And the switch happens because God rises up.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–13 — A Pure Speech and a Humble Remnant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will change the speech of the peoples to a pure speech so that all may call upon the name of the LORD and serve him with one accord (v. 9), with worshippers coming from beyond Cush (v. 10). Shame and haughtiness will be removed, and God will leave a people humble and lowly who seek refuge in the name of the LORD, doing no injustice and speaking no lies (vv. 11-13).
verseByVerse.theology: God's answer to a proud, lying city is a purified people from every nation who take refuge in his name.

verseByVerse.quote: "For at that time I will change the speech of the peoples to a pure speech, that all of them may call upon the name of the LORD and serve him with one accord. From beyond the rivers of Cush my worshipers, the daughter of my dispersed ones, shall bring my offering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For at that time I will change the speech of the peoples to a pure speech, that all of them may call upon the name of the LORD and serve him with one accord.

Watch what God does first in the new world: he changes the way people talk. Chapter 3 began with a city whose speech was corrupt, whose prophets lied and whose priests twisted the law. So God gives a pure speech.

And the purpose is worship: that all of them may call upon the name of the LORD and serve him with one accord. At Babel God confused human language because of human pride (Gen 11:7). Here he unifies it again, not by empire but by making people call on his name together.

The New Testament shows where this began. At Pentecost the Spirit came and people heard the mighty works of God each in their own language (Acts 2:4-11), and Revelation ends with a countless crowd from every nation praising God with one voice (Rev 7:9). What God purifies here, he purifies for singing.

From beyond the rivers of Cush my worshipers, the daughter of my dispersed ones, shall bring my offering.

Worshippers will come from beyond the rivers of Cush, the furthest place Zephaniah's hearers could imagine, deep in Africa. In chapter 2 the Cushites fell under God's sword; now Cushites bring him offerings. God's judgments are never the end of his dealings with a people.

verseByVerse.quote: "On that day you shall not be put to shame because of the deeds by which you have rebelled against me; for then I will remove from your midst your proudly exultant ones, and you shall no longer be haughty in my holy mountain. But I will leave in your midst a people humble and lowly. They shall seek refuge in the name of the LORD, those who are left in Israel; they shall do no injustice and speak no lies, nor shall there be found in their mouth a deceitful tongue. For they shall graze and lie down, and none shall make them afraid."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"On that day you shall not be put to shame because of the deeds by which you have rebelled against me; for then I will remove from your midst your proudly exultant ones, and you shall no longer be haughty in my holy mountain.

Two promises here, and both are precious. First, no shame: you shall not be put to shame because of the deeds by which you have rebelled. The sins are real and are not denied, but the day is coming when they will no longer hang over his people's heads. Christians know why this is possible only because someone else bore the shame.

Second, the removal of the proud from the community of faith. Pride in the church is not a small fault; it is the thing that made Jerusalem unbearable to God.

But I will leave in your midst a people humble and lowly. They shall seek refuge in the name of the LORD,

those who are left in Israel; they shall do no injustice and speak no lies, nor shall there be found in their mouth a deceitful tongue. For they shall graze and lie down, and none shall make them afraid."

Here is the people God is making: humble and lowly, who seek refuge in the name of the LORD. Not strong, not impressive, not the officials or the wealthy; the kind of people chapter 2 addressed as all you humble of the land (2:3).

Jesus began his great sermon with them: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Matt 5:3). And he described himself in the same words: I am gentle and lowly in heart (Matt 11:29). The King is like his people, or rather they are being made like him.

And notice their character: they do no injustice and speak no lies. The corrupt speech of verse 1 has been healed. Then the picture of a flock: they graze and lie down, and none shall make them afraid. A sheep only lies down when it feels safe.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–20 — The LORD Your God Is in Your Midst
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sing aloud, O daughter of Zion, for God has taken away the judgments against her, and The King of Israel, the LORD, is in your midst (vv. 14-15). Fear not: The LORD your God is in your midst, a mighty one who will save; he will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing (vv. 16-17). He will deal with the oppressors, save the lame, gather the outcast and turn their shame into praise (vv. 18-20).
verseByVerse.theology: The book that began with sweeping away ends with God singing over the people he has saved.

verseByVerse.quote: Sing aloud, O daughter of Zion; shout, O Israel! Rejoice and exult with all your heart, O daughter of Jerusalem! The LORD has taken away the judgments against you; he has cleared away your enemies. The King of Israel, the LORD, is in your midst; you shall never again fear evil. On that day it shall be said to Jerusalem: "Fear not, O Zion; let not your hands grow weak. The LORD your God is in your midst, a mighty one who will save; he will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sing aloud, O daughter of Zion; shout, O Israel! Rejoice and exult with all your heart, O daughter of Jerusalem!

Four commands, and every one of them is about joy: Sing aloud, shout, Rejoice, exult with all your heart. This is the city that was called rebellious and defiled a few verses ago. God does not merely forgive her; he tells her to celebrate.

The LORD has taken away the judgments against you; he has cleared away your enemies. The King of Israel, the LORD, is in your midst; you shall never again fear evil.

Three reasons for the singing. The judgments against you are taken away: the legal case is closed. The enemies are cleared away. And best of all, The King of Israel, the LORD, is in your midst.

That last phrase is the gospel in miniature. The problem of the whole book has been a city where God was present but ignored. Now God is present and welcomed, and the result is that you shall never again fear evil. Matthew's Gospel names a child Immanuel, which means God with us (Matt 1:23), and John says the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

On that day it shall be said to Jerusalem: "Fear not, O Zion; let not your hands grow weak.

Fear not, and then a practical word for discouraged people: let not your hands grow weak. Fear makes the hands drop. When you know God is with you, you can pick the work back up.

The LORD your God is in your midst, a mighty one who will save; he will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing.

This is the summit of the book, and one of the most astonishing verses in the Old Testament. Take it phrase by phrase.

The LORD your God is in your midst: not distant, not visiting, but among his people. A mighty one who will save: the word is a warrior's word. His presence is not merely comforting; it is powerful to rescue.

He will rejoice over you with gladness. Most of us can believe that God tolerates us, or forgives us, or is patient with us. That God is glad about us is harder to take in. Yet that is what it says.

He will quiet you by his love. A picture of a parent with an anxious child: the arms go round, and the crying stops. God's love does not merely inform his people; it settles them.

He will exult over you with loud singing. God sings. The Bible tells his people to sing hundreds of times; here God himself sings, and the song is about them. Isaiah says the same: as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you (Isa 62:5). Jesus spoke of joy in heaven over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:7), and endured the cross for the joy that was set before him (Heb 12:2). The joy was his people.

Hold verse 17 next to 1:2, where God said he would sweep everything away. Both are true, and the road from one to the other runs through the cross, where the sweeping fell on Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: I will gather those of you who mourn for the festival, so that you will no longer suffer reproach. Behold, at that time I will deal with all your oppressors. And I will save the lame and gather the outcast, and I will change their shame into praise and renown in all the earth. At that time I will bring you in, at the time when I gather you together; for I will make you renowned and praised among all the peoples of the earth, when I restore your fortunes before your eyes," says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will gather those of you who mourn for the festival, so that you will no longer suffer reproach.

God turns to those who have been grieving that they cannot join the celebrations (the ESV notes the meaning of this verse is uncertain in Hebrew). Exiles far from the temple, the sick, the excluded: God's first act is to gather them.

Behold, at that time I will deal with all your oppressors. And I will save the lame and gather the outcast, and I will change their shame into praise and renown in all the earth.

Three groups, and God has a word for each. The oppressors he will deal with. The lame, who cannot keep up, he will save. The outcast, pushed out of the community, he will gather. Micah made the same promise (Mic 4:6-7).

And then the reversal: I will change their shame into praise and renown in all the earth. The very thing they were ashamed of becomes the reason people praise God. That is what God does with a redeemed life.

At that time I will bring you in, at the time when I gather you together; for I will make you renowned and praised among all the peoples of the earth, when I restore your fortunes before your eyes," says the LORD.

The book ends with a homecoming: I will bring you in, and the restoration happens before your eyes, so that God's people actually see it.

Think of the distance travelled. Zephaniah began with God sweeping the earth bare and searching Jerusalem with lamps. He ends with God gathering the lame, singing over his people, and bringing them home. The same God is speaking in both chapters, and the humble who sought him in 2:3 are the ones he is singing over here.

3.title: He Will Rejoice Over You
3.overview:
Woe to the rebellious, defiled, oppressing city, which listens to no voice, accepts no correction, does not trust the LORD and does not draw near to her God (vv. 1-2). Her officials are roaring lions, her judges evening wolves, her prophets treacherous and her priests profane, doing violence to the law (vv. 3-4). Yet the LORD within her is righteous, showing his justice every morning without fail, while the unjust know no shame (v. 5).

God has cut off nations and left their cities desolate, hoping his people would fear him and accept correction, but they were all the more eager to corrupt their deeds (vv. 6-7). Therefore he tells them to wait for him, for the day when he rises up and pours out his indignation on the nations (v. 8).

Then he will change the speech of the peoples to a pure speech, so that all may call on his name and serve him with one accord, and worshippers will come from beyond the rivers of Cush (vv. 9-10). Shame will be removed and the proud taken away, and God will leave a humble and lowly people who take refuge in his name, doing no injustice and speaking no lies, grazing and lying down with none to make them afraid (vv. 11-13).

Zion is told to sing aloud, for God has taken away the judgments against her and the King of Israel is in her midst (vv. 14-15). Fear not: the LORD your God is in your midst, a mighty one who will save; he will rejoice over you with gladness, quiet you by his love and exult over you with loud singing (vv. 16-17). He will gather the mourners, deal with the oppressors, save the lame, gather the outcast, change shame into praise and bring his people home before their eyes (vv. 18-20).
3.theology:
God's own city can be as guilty as any pagan capital, and its decline shows in deafness, defensiveness, distrust and distance (vv. 1-2).

When leaders in every office fail, God himself remains righteous in the midst of them, faithful as the sunrise (vv. 3-5; Lam 3:22-23).

Warnings that do not soften us harden us (vv. 6-7).

For God's people, the day of judgment is not a threat to dread but a day to wait for (v. 8).

God purifies the speech of the nations so that they call on his name together, reversing Babel and fulfilled from Pentecost onward (v. 9; Gen 11:7; Acts 2:4-11; Rev 7:9).

The people God keeps are humble and lowly, sheltering in his name and made truthful (vv. 12-13; Matt 5:3; 11:29).

God is not merely present but present to save, and his love quiets his people and breaks into singing over them (vv. 15-17; Isa 62:5; Matt 1:23; Luke 15:7; Heb 12:2).

God gathers the lame and the outcast and turns their shame into praise (vv. 19-20; Mic 4:6-7).
3.examples:
A woe aimed at Jerusalem in the same words as one aimed at Nineveh.

Judges described as wolves that leave nothing by morning.

God doing right in the middle of a corrupt city, every single dawn.

Ruined cities on the horizon, meant to be read as a warning.

A command to wait for the day everyone else dreads.

Babel's confusion undone by a purified language of praise.

A parent's arms going round a child until the crying stops.

God himself singing, and the song is about his people.
